land.text: the steppe north of the Gobi, the chanyu's court, seized in the civil war of 57-54 BCE

predecessors.note: A rival chanyu's faction in the Xiongnu civil war; rule 5 (rebel-held land) until Huhanye's victory and Zhizhi's death.

land.text: the steppe north of the Gobi, left to Huhanye in 49 BCE

successors.note: Returned in 49 BCE, before the end year.

land.text: the fortress 'on the Dulaishui River', possibly the Ili or Talas, built by the Kangju for Zhizhi

successors.note: Slug by the slug rule for a state Cliopatria lacks (kangju); the Talas base reverted to it after the Battle of Zhizhi in 36 BCE.

capitals.name: Chanyu's court north of the Gobi (Orkhon)
capitals.note: Held against Huhanye, who 'moved south and submitted to the Chinese' in 53 BCE (Xiongnu page).

capitals.name: Jiankun lands (Minusinsk basin, upper Yenisei)
capitals.note: 'made his capital in the lands of the Jiankun, which may have been the Yenisei Kirghiz' (49 BCE); the point is Abakan, the researcher's placement.

capitals.name: Zhizhi's fortress on the Talas (Taraz)
capitals.note: Killed 'at his capital city (present-day Taraz, Kazakhstan) in 36 BC' (Han-Xiongnu War page); the Zhizhi page has the fortress 'on the Dulaishui River', possibly the Ili or Talas.

correction.text: the steppe north of the Gobi with the chanyu's court, held by Zhizhi while Huhanye sat on the Han frontier

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe (Cliopatria lacks the state). 'In 56 BCE Hutuwusi, elder brother of Huhanye, revolted, called himself Zhizhi Chanyu'; Huhanye 'moved south and submitted to the Chinese' in 53 BCE (Xiongnu page). The extent is the researcher's reading: the court lands north of the Gobi within the Xiongnu shape of 66 BCE.

correction.text: the lands of the Jiankun and the Dingling on the upper Yenisei and beyond Baikal

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. In 49 BCE he 'gained control of the Dingling' and 'made his capital in the lands of the Jiankun'. The Transbaikal part (Dingling) is approximate.

correction.text: the Kangju fortress 'on the Dulaishui River' near the Talas, 'near Lake Balkhash'

keyframe_review.note: New keyframe. In 44 BCE he 'led his entire tribe westward' to Kangju; the Kangju built him a fortress; he 'attacked the Wusun with Kangju allies and extracted tribute from Dayuan'. Drawn as a 150 km radius on Taraz, where the Han-Xiongnu War page places his capital.

region.text: the steppe north of the Gobi, the chanyu's court

ledger.note: 56 BCE: Hutuwusi proclaims himself Zhizhi Chanyu. 'In 56 BCE Hutuwusi, elder brother of Huhanye, revolted, called himself Zhizhi Chanyu' (Zhizhi Chanyu page); the Xiongnu page: 'Runzhen and Zhizhi appeared' in 56, and Zhizhi 'killed Runzhen' in 54 BCE.

region.text: the lands of the Jiankun and the Dingling

ledger.note: 49 BCE: Zhizhi takes the Jiankun and Dingling lands. He 'successfully fought the Wusun' and 'gained control of the Dingling'; he 'made his capital in the lands of the Jiankun, which may have been the Yenisei Kirghiz' (Zhizhi Chanyu page).

region.text: the steppe north of the Gobi

ledger.note: 49 BCE: the court lands north of the Gobi are left to Huhanye, who had Han backing since 53 BCE and visited Chang'an in 51 and 49 BCE (Xiongnu page).
49 BCE: the court moves to the Jiankun lands on the upper Yenisei.

region.text: the lands of the Jiankun and the Dingling

ledger.note: 44 BCE: Zhizhi leaves the Yenisei for Kangju. 'He led his entire tribe westward' to Kangju, near Lake Balkhash, after being reported 'on the north slope of the Tian Shan' (Zhizhi Chanyu page); the Jiankun and Dingling lands revert to their peoples.

region.text: the fortress on the Dulaishui River, 'near Lake Balkhash'

ledger.note: 44 BCE: a base in Kangju. The Kangju were made to build 'a fortress on the Dulaishui River', possibly the Ili or Talas River (undated, after 44 BCE); from it Zhizhi 'attacked the Wusun with Kangju allies and extracted tribute from Dayuan' (Zhizhi Chanyu page).
44 BCE: the court is the fortress on the Talas ('present-day Taraz, Kazakhstan').

region.text: the Kangju city on the Talas

ledger.note: 36 BCE: Zhizhi is killed at the Battle of Zhizhi. 'Zhizhi Chanyu was killed and decapitated' when the Han army under Chen Tang and Gan Yanshou took the Kangju city (Zhizhi Chanyu page); 'his head was sent to Chang'an' (Xiongnu page); 'killed at his capital city (present-day Taraz, Kazakhstan) in 36 BC' (Han-Xiongnu War page).

wars.name: Battle of Zhizhi

zones.text: the Kangju city on the Talas

wars.outcome: Han victory: the city taken, Zhizhi killed and decapitated; the Western Regions' Han officers Chen Tang and Gan Yanshou acted on their own authority.

wars.name: Xiongnu civil war of the five chanyus

zones.text: the steppe north of the Gobi

wars.outcome: Huhanye, backed by Han from 53 BCE, keeps the chanyu's title; Zhizhi withdraws to the Jiankun lands in 49 BCE.

certainty.note: A moving horde: every extent is approximate, the Talas base most of all.

sources.title: Xiongnu
sources.note: The five chanyus 58-54 BCE, Huhanye's submission, Zhizhi's death near Lake Balkhash.

sources.title: Han–Xiongnu War
sources.note: Taraz as Zhizhi's capital city in 36 BCE.

notes: Rebel dossier written by the ia-01-a agent on 2026-10-18 for the rival chanyu of the Xiongnu civil war (rule 5); Cliopatria has no row. Extents are the researcher's readings of three pages: the Orkhon court lands 56-50 BCE, the Jiankun (Minusinsk) and Dingling lands 49-45 BCE, a 150 km radius on Taraz 44-36 BCE. Kangju, Zhizhi's host and the owner of the Talas land after 36 BCE, has no Cliopatria row (counterparts_needing_dossiers). The Battle of Zhizhi page was not opened (budget).
